bottles.reviewSummary: A benchmark lowland blanco: savory, assertive cooked agave with olive brine and pepper, showing more complexity than most in its category.
bottles.producer: Tequila Fortaleza (Fortaleza distillery, Tequila, Jalisco)

bottles.reviewSummary: A welcoming, gently smoky espadín: herbaceous and delicately sweet on the palate, with a long, dry, smoky finish that fades to earthy herbs.
bottles.producer: The Lost Explorer (produced at its Oaxaca palenque)
Vinata Rancho Tepúa (Roberto Contreras, Maestro Bacanorero)
bottles.reviewSummary: Mineral and roast-agave-driven, with sandalwood, cinnamon, lemongrass and a mineral tang around a center of roast agave, over a rich, sweet-agave nose.

bottles.producer: Antonio Arrizon (Maestro Tabernero), La Vieja, Sierra Occidental, Jalisco; brand by Casa Endémica
bottles.reviewSummary: A funky, approachable raicilla: sour apple and a slight vinegar note on the nose, sweet agave and a pleasant fermented funk on the palate — light and easy to sip or mix.

bottles.producer: Roberto Contreras Mayoral (Contreras family vinata, Rancho Tepúa, Aconchi, Sonora)
bottles.batch: Small batches; first premium bacanora legally imported to the US
bottles.reviewSummary: Grassy, sweet agave with a hint of smoke and citrus and a medium-thin body; the smoke comes forward and grassy, earthy notes overtake the initial sweetness. A pleasant, vibrant bacanora overall.
bottles.editorialNote: From the same Contreras family vinata as this profile's example bottle — expect a similarly mineral, pit-roast character, with the Tequila.net review noting smoke that sits forward of the typical profile.

bottles.producer: Rodrigo Bojórquez Bours (family vinata, Álamos, Sonora)
bottles.reviewSummary: Wildflowers, citrus and the tartness of green apple, with a gentle violet finish — an aromatic, moderately complex bacanora.
bottles.editorialNote: A fruitier, more floral read on bacanora than this profile describes — the green-apple tartness and violet finish sit well outside the mineral, savory center of the Rancho Tepúa example.

bottles.producer: La Venenosa (Maestro Tabernero Don Alberto Hernández, El Tuito, Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco)
bottles.reviewSummary: The most savory and smoky offering of the La Venenosa range (lote 32, 2021) — a pour its reviewer found positively delicious at its price point.
bottles.abvNote: ABV not documented in cited sources
bottles.editorialNote: Fits the Costa profile's pit-cooked coastal reading: savory and smoky is exactly what the profile predicts for this style.

bottles.producer: Ignacio Juárez (vinatero, Tuxcacuesco region), Laika Spirits bottling
bottles.reviewSummary: A rich nose with spicy, pickle-juice and tangy notes (Mezcalistas); lime zest, hay, peppercorn and agave on a straightforward, mineral palate (Mezcal Reviews members).
bottles.abvNote: ABV not documented in cited sources

bottles.producer: Comiteco Córdova & Guillén (Comitán de Domínguez, Chiapas)
bottles.composition: Distilled from fermented agave sap (aguamiel); the broader comiteco category permits an additional cane-based sugar source — whether this specific bottle is 100% agave is not documented in the cited sources
bottles.reviewSummary: Mezcal Reviews lists 9 Guardianes Comiteco Blanco from maguey Comitlán sap fermented and distilled in copper; tasting-note detail for this specific expression is not yet documented.
bottles.abvNote: ABV not documented in cited sources
bottles.classification: Comiteco — joven (no legal aging classes; sap-only 100% agave, per the producer)
bottles.plantComposition: Fermented and double-distilled from fresh aguamiel of maguey comiteco (Agave atrovirens); per the producer's US importer, glass-rested about six months before bottling

bottles.producer: Razo family / Rodolfo de Razo (Rancho San Isidro collective, Nanacamilpa, Tlaxcala)
bottles.reviewSummary: Green and vegetal, with curious notes of cardamom, lemongrass, peppercorn, sharp cheddar and sorrel — double-distilled from 48-hour fermented Salmiana sap in a short copper column, per importer notes.

bottles.producer: Tequila Fortaleza (Fortaleza distillery, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.batch: Aged in American oak; lots vary
bottles.reviewSummary: An earthy palate of cinnamon, caramel and citrus with olive and butter notes from 6–8 months in American oak; the clean agave of the blanco stays intact, accented by soft oakiness and wood spice.

bottles.producer: Tequila Fortaleza (Fortaleza distillery, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.batch: Aged ~18 months in ex-bourbon casks
bottles.reviewSummary: White-sugar and honey sweetness, pineapple, green grape and vegetal agave over gentle barrel fruitiness — darker and rounder than the blanco, with oak woven in rather than dominant.

bottles.producer: Patrón (Hacienda Patrón, Jalisco)
bottles.batch: Añejo aged in American and French oak, then charcoal-filtered clear
bottles.reviewSummary: Round, creamy aromas and flavors — vanilla, oak charcoal, lemon cream, toasted pineapple — with softer acidity and agave than a blanco; an easy-sipping profile of light agave, oak, cinnamon and vanilla.

bottles.producer: Comiteco Córdova & Guillén (Comitán de Domínguez, Chiapas)
bottles.batch: Rested in glass with branches of white oak
bottles.composition: Distilled from fermented agave sap (aguamiel); the broader comiteco category permits an additional cane-based sugar source — whether this specific bottle is 100% agave is not documented in the cited sources
bottles.reviewSummary: Mezcal Reviews lists 9 Guardianes Comiteco Añejo at 42% ABV, from maguey Comitlán sap fermented and distilled in copper, then aged; the site lists no tasting notes for this expression, so no flavor description is offered beyond the profile-relative editorial note.
bottles.classification: Comiteco — añejo (no legal aging classes; the wood character comes from glass-resting, per the producer)
bottles.plantComposition: Fermented and double-distilled from fresh aguamiel of maguey comiteco (Agave atrovirens); per the producer's US importer, rested in glass with white-oak branches rather than barrels

bottles.producer: Tabernas Edición line (batch producers vary; Antonio Arrizon, Benito Salcedo Rios, José Salcedo listed by the review source), Sierra Occidental, Jalisco
bottles.abvNote: ABV varies by batch (review source lists a 44.8% batch; a 40-46% range is documented) — check the bottle
bottles.batch: Rested about 3 months in wooden (sherry) casks; each Tabernas Edición batch differs — check your bottle
bottles.reviewSummary: Vanilla, caramel, leather, sweet tobacco and plum on the nose; plum, raisin, luxardo cherry, vanilla and leather on the palate, finishing with sweet campfire smoke, cinnamon and tobacco. The sherry-cask influence is fun, though its reviewer notes it overpowers the agave a bit.

bottles.producer: Gerónimo Rosainz (master distiller; brand by Jorge Viveros), northeast Tlaxcala village
bottles.batch: Single distilled in stainless steel; aguamiel fermented about a week with pulque madre
bottles.reviewSummary: A beguiling nose of lightly fermented tepache, mango and molasses richness; on the palate hints of licorice and fennel with a lactic blast, and a fantastic tension between sweet and savory.

bottles.producer: Comiteco 9 Guardianes line (Don Elias in Mexico), Comitán de Domínguez, Chiapas
bottles.batch: Aguamiel and cane spirit; per the review source this label is an aguamiel and cane spirit, unlike the 100%-sap 9 Guardianes label
bottles.composition: Distilled from fermented agave sap (aguamiel) blended with cane-based spirit; the non-agave component is disclosed on the label and by the cited source — included as a factual entry, not as a comiteco style profile
bottles.reviewSummary: Neat, it would substitute cleanly for white rum in a mojito — of the two Chiapanecan spirits its reviewer tasted that day, the comiteco was the preferred pour.

bottles.producer: La Alteña Distillery (Camarena family, Carlos Camarena), Jalisco highlands
bottles.place: Jalisco highlands (La Alteña, near Arandas), Jalisco
bottles.batch: Aged 4-5 years in American oak ex-bourbon barrels — longer than the 3-year legal minimum
bottles.reviewSummary: Keeps the agave clearly in the frame where most extra añejos are caramel-vanilla bombs: an herbal nose of rosemary, pepper and allspice that could pass for a reposado, over deep oak.

bottles.producer: Ilegal Mezcal (Tlacolula valley producers; brand by John Rexer), Oaxaca
bottles.batch: Joven espadín rested about 4-6 months in American oak (ex-whiskey casks per brand notes)
bottles.reviewSummary: Smooth, with a subtle straw-like aroma, hints of citrus and candy sweetness; vanilla and citrus on the palate with spice and earth, and a sweet, smooth finish. A second review adds clove and butterscotch, with the smoke carrying from nose to a smoky-butterscotch finish.

bottles.producer: Ilegal Mezcal (Tlacolula valley producers; brand by John Rexer), Oaxaca
bottles.batch: Joven espadín rested about 14 months in American oak, beyond the 1-year añejo minimum
bottles.reviewSummary: Leans further into caramel and spicier wood notes than the reposado, with less of the joven's smoke — one reviewer's most pleasing aged-mezcal surprise; Bourbon Banter describes the same caramel-and-wood direction.
bottles.editorialNote: An añejo (rested about 14 months, beyond the 1-year añejo minimum): the app's aged-mezcal profile describes the reposado class (2 months to 1 year), so this expression is covered as a catalogue fact, not mapped onto the reposado style profile.

bottles.producer: Montelobos (mezcalero Iván Saldaña; produced at Palenque del Tentzo), Puebla
bottles.abvNote: ABV varies by lot; the cited review lists lot-specific notes — check your bottle
bottles.place: San Nicolás Huajuapan (Palenque del Tentzo), Puebla
bottles.batch: 100% cultivated tobalá (no wild-harvest), pit-roasted; sustainability-focused production
bottles.reviewSummary: Aromas of lemon, green pepper and pear, with citrus, basil, roasted fig, macadamia and truffle on the palate; member notes across lots also mention bubblegum and fresh-cut grass.
bottles.editorialNote: Cultivated tobalá from Puebla, outside the wild-Oaxaca Sierra context this profile describes; the plant is the same species, but the growing region and cultivated production differ.

bottles.producer: Macurichos (maestro mezcalero Gonzalo Martinez), Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca
bottles.abvNote: Small-batch ABV varies (a cited member review lists a 47.54% batch); check your bottle
bottles.batch: Ancestral production: earthen-oven cooked, tahona-milled, wooden-vat fermented, clay pot stills; family also reforests wild populations
bottles.reviewSummary: Herbal, with notes of dry soil, thyme, coriander and a touch of rosemary; a member review found it soft and delicate, with solid sweetness throughout.

bottles.producer: Del Maguey Single Village (Florencio Carlos Sarmiento and family), Santa Catarina Minas, Oaxaca
bottles.abvNote: ABV varies by batch (a cited retail listing shows 49%); check your bottle
bottles.batch: Triple-distilled; the third distillation passes vapor through wild mountain fruits, almonds, rice and a suspended raw chicken breast (pechuga); seasonal, limited production
bottles.reviewSummary: Black licorice, anise and clove with fruit and a Scotch-like smokiness — and, yes, a taste of chicken; other notes find basil, lemon, ocean and fruit on the nose, with smoky roast chicken skin, paprika and sea salt in a second review. A festival-production style, not an everyday class.
bottles.editorialNote: Pechuga is a festival-production style (a third distillation over fruit, rice and a suspended raw chicken breast), not a typical joven espadín; it is contextual to mezcal tradition rather than representative of this profile.

bottles.producer: Siete Pozos Taberna (maestro tabernero Refugio Pineda Cruz; brand owner Luis Velasco), Zapotitlán de Vadillo, Jalisco
bottles.abvNote: Small-batch production; ABV varies (a retail listing shows 45%) — check your bottle
bottles.batch: Wild ixtero amarillo and lineño agaves, pit-roasted, volcanic-stone fermented, copper distilled; one of the producers actively pushing for a tuxca denomination of origin
bottles.reviewSummary: A sweet floral fragrance with light sandalwood (batch 03), a lactic palate with green peppers and sweet minerality, and an agave-rich finish.

bottles.producer: Indio Alonso (fifth-generation tuxquero David Benítez Venegas), Zapotitlán de Vadillo, Jalisco
bottles.abvNote: Small-batch production; ABV not documented in the cited source — check your bottle
bottles.batch: Wild cimarrón (Agave angustifolia), cuaquizoca and salmiana (Agave inaequidens) agaves, pit-roasted, volcanic-stone-pit fermented, copper double-distilled; another producer pushing for a tuxca denomination of origin
bottles.reviewSummary: The cited Mezcal Reviews entry documents the multi-agave composition (cimarrón, cuaquizoca, salmiana) and the volcanic-stone-pit fermentation; tasting notes for this specific batch are not yet documented, so no flavor character is claimed here.

bottles.producer: Bienvenido Fernandez (40+ years' experience; learned in clandestine vinatas of the northern Chihuahuan Sierra), Chihuahua
bottles.abvNote: ABV varies by batch (a cited member review lists 46.5% for a March 2018 lot); check your bottle
bottles.batch: Small batches from wild Dasylirion; the color-coded Clande labels each mark a different sotolero — the yellow label is Bienvenido Fernandez
bottles.reviewSummary: Pure magic in aroma and flavor for its reviewers — one called it their favorite sotol tried thus far; the brand's terroir-driven project supports small local producers and Dasylirion conservation.

bottles.producer: Vinomex (master distiller José Daumas Gil de Partearroyo), Delicias, Chihuahua
bottles.abvNote: ABV not stated on the cited review page; the producer's aged line is lower-ABV per member notes — check your bottle
bottles.batch: 100% wild-harvested Dasylirion, steam-cooked, triple-distilled in double-column copper, then aged 2 years in new French white oak; USDA organic and Kosher certified
bottles.reviewSummary: A medicinal-herbal character with brown sugar and anise and a very slight bitter finish — a light summer sipper its reviewer found comparable to fine añejo tequilas but deeper.
bottles.editorialNote: An aged sotol (2 years in new French oak): the app's sotol profile describes an unaged Chihuahua desert style with no oak maturation, so this expression is covered as a catalogue fact, not mapped onto that style profile.

bottles.producer: Bacatt (small-batch Sonoran bacanora), Sonora
bottles.abvNote: Small-lot production; ABV varies (the cited review is from lot 2305) — check your bottle
bottles.batch: Traditional underground-oven roasted maguey pacifica; lot 2305, bottle 242 of the cited run
bottles.reviewSummary: Wet grass after a rainstorm, woody sweetness and minerality on the nose; the palate shifts between a sweet mesquite-oak note with a minty finish and a peppery cookies-and-cream note — a bottle its reviewer now saves for special occasions.

bottles.producer: Sunora (small-batch, several generations of bacanora makers), Sonora
bottles.abvNote: ABV not documented on the cited review page — check your bottle
bottles.batch: Maguey pacifica roasted 48 hours in underground ovens (mallas), stone-wheel crushed, fermented 6-12 days, triple-distilled
bottles.reviewSummary: Jalapeño, watermelon and cream cheese with roasted agave piña and sourdough on the nose; grilled artichoke, charred asparagus, wet stone and a turkey-jerky meatiness on the palate, with a light earthy smoke — a solid introduction to the category.

bottles.producer: Rafael Encinas (double-distillation), San Pedro de la Cueva, Sonora
bottles.abvNote: Small-batch production; ABV varies (the cited review lists 48% for batch B002) — check your bottle
bottles.place: San Pedro de la Cueva, Sonora
bottles.batch: Handcrafted small batches from agave pacifica; cited batch B002, bottle 909/1000
bottles.reviewSummary: Briny and viscous, with fruit and agave sugar; one member note found cotton candy on the nose, orange fancy-toothpaste and buttercream notes, and a slight sour finish.

bottles.producer: Taberna 3 Gallos (producer Fausto, chemical engineer; Labastida family tradition), Jalisco
bottles.batch: Unaged plata from Taberna 3 Gallos; homage to the harvest celebrations of Hacienda de Ahuacatepec
bottles.reviewSummary: Bright aromatics of green bell pepper and grass with jalapeño and red bell pepper, and a grass-driven palate of agave, green apple and jalapeño — the top-ranked agave spirit (97/100) at the 2025 Beverage Testing Institute judging, per Tastings.com and Forbes.

bottles.producer: Aguamiel Bacanora (Quintana family vináta, Suaqui Grande, Sonora)
bottles.classification: Bacanora — blanco (unaged); Sonora denomination of origin
bottles.plantComposition: 100% wild agave yaquiana/Pacifica (the Sonoran form of Agave angustifolia), per the producer
bottles.reviewSummary: Warm agave with vanilla cake and slight fruit (pineapple, banana cream) on the nose, then a sweet, juicy palate with whipped-cream, cake-batter and custard notes against slight grass, smoke and salinity.

bottles.producer: Don Julio (Tequila Tres Magueyes, Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco)
bottles.reviewSummary: A peppery, mineral nose with zesty lemon and pink grapefruit and subtle yeasty pastry aromas; the clean, mineral palate offers fudge, pastry and delicate herbal flavours, ending in a long, dry finish with vegetal notes and spicy black pepper. Un-aged, rested briefly in inert containers before bottling.
bottles.editorialNote: A highlands blanco rather than a Tequila Valley one: expect the brighter, fruitier highland reading of the same legal class.

bottles.producer: Jose Cuervo (La Rojeña distillery, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.reviewSummary: Fruitiness, spice and pepper held back compared with earlier bottlings — still a pleasant, easy reposado, but with less punchy agave than its reviewer wants in a sipped tequila.

bottles.producer: PATRÓN (Hacienda Patrón, Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco)
bottles.reviewSummary: A lovely vegetal aroma of cooked agave — grass, green peppers, a little earth and eucalyptus — with flavors of agave, eucalyptus and white pepper leading to a smooth, savory finish; fine neat and in cocktails, if priced as a premium.
bottles.editorialNote: A highlands blanco: the same unaged class as the featured valley example, with the highlands' fruitier, more citric reading.

bottles.producer: Casa Dragones (small-batch distilling, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), per the brand
bottles.reviewSummary: Fresh grapefruit and green apple on the nose, agave forward on the sip with black pepper, cloves, mint and juicy tropical fruit, finishing light and bright with grapefruit, pepper and cooling herbs.

bottles.producer: G4 (Felipe Camarena, El Pandillo distillery, NOM 1579, Jesús María, Jalisco)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), estate grown
bottles.batch: Made with a 50/50 blend of rainwater and spring water; stone-oven cooked and tahona-crushed
bottles.reviewSummary: Showcases the complex, savory delights of highland agave, oozing pepper and green olive notes; the producer's method — slow stone-oven cooking, a handmade metal tahona, double distillation in copper — keeps the agave front and center.

bottles.producer: Maestro Dobel (Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Tequila — cristalino-style extra añejo (oak-aged 3+ years, filtered to remove color)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), per the producer
bottles.batch: Aged a minimum of three years in American and Eastern European oak, then charcoal-filtered clear
bottles.reviewSummary: A smooth, complex cristalino: the oak's richness carries through the filtration, with fig, quince, date, pineapple and pumpkin notes over cinnamon, vanilla and clove noted by the producer.

bottles.producer: Tequila Cascahuín (Rosales family, NOM 1123, El Arenal, Jalisco)
bottles.abvNote: ABV not documented in the cited reviews; the distillery's standard bottling is around 40% — check your bottle
bottles.batch: Rested 14–16 months in well-seasoned American oak (barrels with long tequila-maturation history), per the producer's US importer
bottles.reviewSummary: Keeps cooked agave at the center with oak in support — the house's earthy, mineral valley character holding on under gentle barrel sweetness.

bottles.producer: Tequila Ocho (Carlos Camarena, Tequilera Los Alambiques, NOM 1474, Arandas, Jalisco)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), single-estate and vintage-dated
bottles.batch: Vintage-dated from a single rancho; aged a minimum of three years in ex-American whiskey barrels
bottles.reviewSummary: Cherries, anise, dark chocolate, sherry, oak and plantain on the nose, and oak, anise, dried fruit, cherries, toffee, black pepper and cinnamon on the palate. No independent review of the current release is documented; per the producer's own notes.

bottles.producer: Balam (Maestro Tabernero Don Rosalio Rodríguez, El Tuito, Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Raicilla — joven (unaged); Jalisco denomination of origin
bottles.plantComposition: Agave Chino Aguiar / rhodacantha, per the producer's listing; batch composition varies

bottles.producer: Don Julio (Tequila Tres Magueyes, Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Tequila — 100% agave reposado (oak-rested 8 months, per the review)
bottles.reviewSummary: Smooth complexity throughout: a fade of butterscotch, nutty almond and a smattering of wood-spice and tea, with peppery spices building in the throat.
bottles.editorialNote: A highlands reposado: the app's reposado profile describes the Tequila Valley reading, and this expression distills in Los Altos — covered here as a catalogue fact, not mapped onto the valley profile.

bottles.producer: Don Julio (Tequila Tres Magueyes, Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Tequila — 100% agave añejo (oak-aged 18 months, per the cited taste test)
bottles.reviewSummary: Mellow agave with mild white pepper and light caramel, a very mild oak presence and an appealing honey-like sweetness, with lime zest and apricot jam melded into the agave, oak and caramel.
bottles.editorialNote: A highlands añejo: the app's añejo profile describes the Tequila Valley reading, and this expression distills in Los Altos — covered here as a catalogue fact, not mapped onto the valley profile.

bottles.producer: Jose Cuervo (La Rojeña / Casa Cuervo, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.reviewSummary: An easy-drinking silver with the valley's earthy, herbaceous character present but gentler than the category's punchiest examples — released in 2011 as a true 100% blue agave tequila from the central lowland region.

bottles.producer: PATRÓN (Hacienda Patrón, NOM 1492, Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Tequila — 100% agave reposado (oak-rested, average about six months per the review)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana); a blend of tahona-crushed and roller-mill tequilas, per the producer profile
bottles.reviewSummary: A dichotomous spirit: honeyed caramel sweetness, soft earthy baked squash, sweet green peppers, hot white pepper, sandalwood and a hint of vanilla, changing direction on the first sip.
bottles.editorialNote: A highlands reposado: the app's reposado profile describes the Tequila Valley reading, and this expression distills in Los Altos — covered here as a catalogue fact, not mapped onto the valley profile.

bottles.producer: Casa Dragones (small-batch master blend, Tequila, Jalisco)
bottles.classification: Tequila — joven (a master blend of silver with a hint of extra añejo, filtered to platinum clarity)
bottles.plantComposition: 100% blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), per the brand
bottles.reviewSummary: Extraordinarily smooth, with a very sweet, fruity, almost wine-like nose and a bold, pure peppery flavor that finishes cleanly.
bottles.editorialNote: A joven blend: no joven tequila style profile exists in this guide yet, so this entry is covered as a catalogue fact only.
